newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia energy sector may strain to find investors.
newsitem.headline: Russia energy sector may strain to find investors.

text.p: Russia will struggle to attract long-term investment to its ailing oil and gas sectors while returns on its financial markets are high, Andrei Konoplyanik, an adviser to parliament's lower house, said on Tuesday.

He also said that the list being scrutinised by the State Duma of oil and gas reserves viable for exploitation under production sharing agreements in Russia had been reduced to 23 deposits from 213 last May.

"Private investors are investing in Russia's financial and stock markets, and there are not enough long term private investors ready to invest in the oil and gas sector," he told an industry conference.
Konoplyanik said rates of return on Russia's financial and stock markets had been higher than returns on these markets in the West.
The Russian Trading System share index closed at 288.63 on Tuesday, off a high of 349.27 on February 20. But it has risen from below 200 at the end of last year.
"Only when we see securities in Russia down to the rates seen on Western markets can we expect an influx of investment into oil and gas," he said.
He said domestic investment in the oil industry would not be enough to reverse the production slide seen in recent years, and that government support for the energy sector was paltry.

"We should forget the state sector as a source of investment in the oil and gas sector," he said, adding that only 1.4 trillion roubles ($250 million) had been earmarked for the sector in this year's federal budget.

He estimated the cost of developing the 23 reserves on the preliminary production sharing list at around $53 billion. The cost of developing all 213 reserves on the list from May last year would be about $132 billion.
Konoplyanik said that production sharing laws were the only viable path to a recovery in oil investment, and in turn production. Russian output has nearly halved since the 1980s.
"The only possible mechanism is to pass the (production sharing) laws, and there is no alternative to this path," he said.

The conservative-dominated Duma has held up passing the list of reserves viable for production sharing agreements, as well as legislative changes required to make the existing production sharing law compatible with Russian law.

Some Duma members argue that Russia risks handing over natural resources wealth to foreign companies too cheaply, while Western oil executives say that without their participation in major projects, the decline in Russian oil output will continue.
